    How to make a mandala DXF

    1. Design it. Start from a design above, press Surprise me, or draw your own. Straight shapes like spikes and diamonds cut cleanest.
    2. Pick a style. Under Get your cut file, keep Laser, CNC or plasma and choose Cut-ready outlines, Stencil or Centerlines.
    3. Set size and thickness. Enter the finished width and a line thickness your material can hold.
    4. Check, then download. The count under the design tells you how many separate pieces it cuts into at that size and thickness, so you can fix loose shapes before you cut.

    Line thickness by machine

    Machine and materialStarting line thickness
    Plasma, 16 to 14 gauge steel0.08 to 0.125 in (2 to 3 mm) or more
    Laser, 3 mm plywood or acrylic0.06 to 0.08 in (1.5 to 2 mm)
    CNC routerWider than your bit diameter

    These are starting points. A common plasma rule of thumb is to keep lines and bridges at least as wide as the material is thick. Always test on scrap.

    Before you cut

    • Kerf. Draw at finished size and let your CAM software apply the kerf offset.
    • Loose pieces. Anything that doesn't touch another line drops out. Overlap shapes or add rings to tie them in.
    • Heat. Dense designs on thin sheet can warp. Spread the cut order around the part.

    Read the full guide: How to laser or plasma cut a mandala.

    Questions

    Which DXF style should I use?

    Cut-ready outlines keep your lines as solid material, for filigree pieces and wall art. Stencil cuts the design out of a solid disc, for panels and lantern sides. Centerlines are single lines for engraving, scoring or pen plotters.

    What units does the DXF use?

    Inches or millimeters, whichever you choose. The design is scaled so its outside edge is exactly the width you enter, and the file header records the units.

    Will it open in my software?

    The DXF uses simple closed polylines, which LightBurn, Fusion, Inkscape, SheetCAM and most other CAD and CAM programs read.
